8. STAFF ADMINISTRATIVE ITEMS
A. Receive Updates and Take Action to Advance Racial Equity Efforts in Our Community
Recommended Action
Staff recommends that the City Council receive an update on racial equity work undertaken in Santa Monica since June 9, 2020, and direct staff to take the following actions:
Advancing a Black Agenda for Santa Monica
· Develop a mechanism to provide $100,000 in seed funding to advance the formation of a non-profit organization to promote the wellbeing of the Black community in Santa Monica, including people who live, work, and visit Santa Monica , and to build a more equitabl e and just Sant a Monica;
· Host a community forum in collaboration with the Black Agenda for Santa Monica Steering Committee to provide education across the Santa Monica community regarding the history of the Black community in Santa Monica, implicit bias, and ways commun ity members can join togethe r to advance anti-racism in Santa Monica;
Equity and Inclusion Work within the City Organization
· Authorize the formation of a Racial Equity Committee within the City organization and the appointment of an existing staff member i n each City department to se rve as an Equity and Inclusion Officer and member of this Committee;
· Adopt the Racial Equity Statement developed by staff participants in the Government Allianc e on Race and Equity
Public Safety Reform
· Return with a draft ordina nce to create and establish a nine-member Police Engagement and Accountability Commission;
· Review and revise Santa Monica Police Department (SMPD) use of force policies to explicitly a ffirm that all public safety officers must hold the highe st regard for t he sanctity of human life an d the dignity and liberty of all persons and place minimal reliance on the use of force;
· Develop a regular SMPD training schedule focused on equitable and i nclusive policing, and make information about this traini ng program as w ell as officer wellbeing pro grams and policies available to the public on the SMPD website;
· Review proposed recommendations for alternate dispatch approaches and return with a proposal to (a) direct the public to an easy-to-identify non-emer gency line, (b) reduce the number of minor calls serviced by sworn officers and refer them instead to alternative response personnel, and (c) explore third-party partnerships to implement crisis inte rvention teams similar to those employed in the Eugene, O regon CAHOOTS p rogram;
· Increase the numb er of SMPD officers assigned as Neighborhood Resource Officers from four to eight;
· Request an additional Los Angeles County Department of Mental Health (DMH ) resource to work with the SMPD Homeless Liaison Program (HLP) and assi gn an officer to work with t hat DMH resource;
· Take steps through the budget process to achieve more balanced investment of City resources across all departments responsible for provid ing direct services to promote community wellbeing.

  CITY OF SANTA MONICA

  CITY COUNCIL MINUTES

  SEPTEMBER 8, 2020

  A regular meeting of the Santa Monica City Council was called to order by Mayor McKeown at 5:30 p.m., on
  Tuesday, September 8, 2020, via teleconference pursuant to the Governor’s Executive Order N-29-20 at
  https://primetime.bluejeans.com/a2m/live-event/ebjxxpjs

  Councilmember Ted Winterer

  Interim City Attorney George Cardona
  City Clerk Denise Anderson-Warren

  CONVENE  On order of the Mayor, the City Council convened at 5:30 p.m., with all
  members present.

  CLOSED SESSIONS  There was no one present for public comment on closed sessions.

  On order of the Mayor, the City Council recessed at 5:36 p.m., to consider
  closed sessions and returned at 6:45 p.m., with all members present, to report
  the following:

  1.A. Conference with Legal Counsel – Anticipated Litigation – Request
  to enter into a lawsuit as an amicus curiae, pursuant to Government Code
  Section 54956.9: Washington v. United States Postal Service, Eastern
  District of Washington, Case No. 20-cv-03127; New York v. United States
  Postal Services, District of Columbia, Case No. 20-cv-02340; Pennsylvania
  v. DeJoy, Eastern District of Pennsylvania, Case No. 20-cv-04096.

  The Interim City Attorney advised these lawsuits challenge a series of
  policies implemented by the U.S. Postmaster General that have delayed mail
  delivery, alleging that these changes violate statutory requirements and the
  26th Amendment, which forbids age discrimination in voting, and infringe on
  states’ constitutional authority to regulate elections. The County of Santa
  Clara and Public Rights Project, on behalf of the City of Columbus, are

  1  September 8, 2020

  authoring an amicus brief on behalf of City and County governments
  supporting these challenges by focusing on the current and potential impacts
  of delayed mail service on the administration of elections by local
  governments. The City Attorney’s Office recommends joining in the amicus
  brief as filed in one or more of these cases.

  Motion by Councilmember Davis, seconded by Councilmember Jara, to
  approve joining the amicus brief. The motion was approved by the following
  vote:

  AYES:  Councilmembers McCowan, Himmelrich, Davis, Winterer, Jara,
  Mayor Pro Tem O’Day, Mayor McKeown
  NOES:  None
  ABSENT: None

  has been initiated formally pursuant to Government Code Section
  54956.9(d)(1): Carrie Papillion v. City of Santa Monica, Los Angeles
  Superior Court, Case No. 19STCV07861.

  The Interim City Attorney advised this was a Big Blue Bus injury that Ms.
  Papillion claims the door closed on her. The City does not admit to the
  allegations made in the lawsuit, but to avoid the expense and burden of
  litigation, the City Attorney recommended settlement in the amount of
  $36,000.

  Motion by Councilmember Himmelrich, seconded by Councilmember
  McCowan, to approve Settlement No. 11103 (CCS) in the amount of $36,000.
  The motion was approved by the following vote:

  AYES:  Councilmembers Jara, Winterer, Davis, Himmelrich, McCowan,
  Mayor Pro Tem O’Day, Mayor McKeown
  NOES:  None
  ABSENT: None

  has been initiated formally pursuant to Government Code Section
  54956.9(d)(1): John JB Doe, et al. v. City of Santa Monica, et al., Los
  Angeles Superior Court, Case No. 20STCV28431.

  The Interim City Attorney advised this matter was heard with no reportable
  action taken.

  54956.9(d)(1): Bermudez v. City of Santa Monica, et al., Case No.

  The Interim City Attorney advised this matter the plaintiff alleges that she

  Bus. The City does not admit to the allegations made in the lawsuit, but to
  avoid the expense and burden of litigation, the City Attorney recommended

  Case No. 20-cv-01105; New York, et al. v. HHS, Southern District of New
  York, Case No. 20-cv-05583.

  The Interim City Attorney advised these lawsuits were brought about by a
  number of states, including the State of California, challenging the Department
  of Health and Human Services, June 2020 final rule that eliminates gender
  identity from the definition of sex, and instead define sex to be the biological
  bindery male and female. The City of Chicago and the County of Santa Clara
  are offering an amicus brief on behalf of cities and counties, supporting the
  claims that HHS violated the Administrative Procedures Act by acting in an
  arbitrary, capricious, and unlawful manner in ignoring the harms imposed by
  withdrawing non-discrimination protections related to healthcare for many of
  their most at-risk residents. The City Attorney’s Office recommends joining in
  the amicus brief as filed by one of these cases.

  Motion by Councilmember Davis, seconded by Councilmember Himmelrich,
  to direct staff to: develop a regular SMPD training schedule based on the
  recommendations of the Public Safety Reform Advisory Committee, related to
  training laid out on pages 18 and 19:
  • All police training must be posted on the SMPD website. The date, subject,
  and duration of the training must be posted for all training in the last six years.
  A schedule of upcoming training must be posted as well.
  • The police must tie each training to a specific and measurable outcome. The
  police and Civilian Oversight Board will work together to determine the
  outcomes and the timeframe to achieve those outcomes.
  • Scenario training is preferred to classroom training, which is preferred to
  video based, self-paced training. Officer duties can include high-adrenaline
  scenarios and their training should match those scenarios. Adults retain a small
  amount of information in classroom settings and when you add a high-
  adrenaline workplace, classroom training proves to be even less effective.
  • Police must partake in each of the following training sessions twice a year.
  - Implicit Bias/Critical Race Theory
  - Participation in Restorative Justice
  - Adolescent Development
  - Violence and De-escalation
  - Mental Health Awareness
  - Trauma Response
  - Transgender Awareness
  - Santa Monica History - Police & the Community
  • For the above training, during one of the two sessions in a given year, the
  training will have a restorative justice component where members of the
  community come into the police station and participate in restorative
  conversations. If training with community members has to be cut short, it must
  be made up within a 3-month period. If necessary, the training can take place
  during roll call.
  • In addition to the current support offered to officers (Chaplain, Peer,
  Therapist), it will be mandatory that officers attend a one-hour session with a
